author: tx
cardQuote: Yet they want to build a giant sink of answers for technical problems. That sink already exists, it's called Internet
quote:
Am I the only one who feels that problem they're trying to solve does not exist? Perhaps I read too many books or perhaps my googling skills are bad ass, but finding information on programming issues is not hard and nothing, and I mean it, beats IRC: simple to use, two-way, ad-free, HTML/JavaScript-free, text-only instant and real-time solution to all your problems.

Yet they want to build a giant sink of answers for technical problems. That sink already exists, it's called Internet: post an answer to any question on millions of message boards, google groups ans sites like news.yc. Internet has has an awesome search facility built-in - people will find what you said.

Search for this on google: "The author of this, David Beazley" and you'll get news.yc page with someone's comment containing those words only 4 (!) hours ago (from this moment as I'm writing this).

Why another site? Sure, they have the blogging powers to hype the hell out of their project, but come on...
storyTitle: StackOverflow.com : the new venture from Joel Spolsky
outcomeDetail: Stack Overflow launched in September 2008, became the default answer engine for working programmers, and Prosus bought it for $1.8B in 2021. The company also runs Stack Exchange and Stack Overflow for Teams.
note: tx was right that the internet already had answers. He was wrong that a structured, ranked, maintained archive would not beat scattered forums and IRC logs.

author: jrockway
cardQuote: I have a feeling this will end up going the way of the prostitution section on Craigslist, or that site where you could offer to carpool with someone to work.
quote:
I have a feeling this will end up going the way of the prostitution section on Craigslist, or that site where you could offer to carpool with someone to work.

The entrenched businesses don't want any competition from this here new-fangled internets.
storyTitle: Travel like a human (Airbnb, YC W09)
outcome: IPO in 2020. 5M+ hosts and 2B+ guest arrivals.
outcomeDetail: Airbnb fought city-by-city regulation, survived the pandemic, and went public in December 2020. By 2024 it had passed 2 billion guest arrivals.
note: The Craigslist analogy assumed Airbnb would be a shady classifieds board. It became a trust-and-payments layer for spare rooms.

author: jganetsk
cardQuote: So, that means Dropbox is going to have to resell S3 at a premium for the added value of these nice Coda-like features. Would you pay a premium for these Dropbox features?
quote:
Look at the prices for S3:

 $0.15 per GB-Month of storage used.
 $0.20 per GB of data transferred.

So, that means Dropbox is going to have to resell S3 at a premium for the added value of these nice Coda-like features. Would you pay a premium for these Dropbox features? Maybe, I don't know.

Also, what's the typical use case? How much bandwidth/storage are people going to consume? Because, if I store 100 megabytes... my bill will pennies every month (going on S3 prices). You cannot transact pennies per user per month. If you could, then you've cracked the micropayments problem wide open. Maybe there would be a base fee? Like $5/month or something. Would people pay that much for online storage? 

I don't know how other revenue generation models can be applied. Advertising? Selling a user's data to other businesses? (What's the privacy policy?)
storyTitle: My YC app: Dropbox - Throw away your USB drive
outcomeDetail: Dropbox moved off S3, built its own storage, and went public in 2018. It became the default sync folder for hundreds of millions of users.
note: The early unit economics really were ugly. Dropbox's answer was scale, its own infrastructure, and a freemium funnel, not reselling S3 forever.

author: jondubois
cardQuote: Performance-wise, full server-side rendering is a huge step back. For dynamic web apps, next.js is going to drive up hosting costs massively and open you up to DDoS attacks because of server-side cache issues.
quote:
The second point "Shared data between requests" would actually turn into a negative when it comes to dynamic web apps; if you had to re-render a component in realtime and send the HTML for that component over the wire for every permutation and change of data (which will be different for each user), caching would be futile.
Also, this will basically move cache consumption from the client to the server; which is worse for the company which has to pay for hosting.

Performance-wise, full server-side rendering is a huge step back. For dynamic web apps, next.js is going to drive up hosting costs massively and open you up to DDoS attacks because of server-side cache issues. I suppose it's OK for static websites.
storyTitle: Next.js – A small framework for server-rendered universal JavaScript apps
outcome: Used by Nike, TikTok, and Hulu; millions of weekly downloads.
outcomeDetail: Next.js made server rendering and file-system routing mainstream again, became Vercel's flagship framework, and powers production sites for Nike, TikTok, and Hulu.
note: The caching and cost critique was real. Incremental static regeneration, edge caching, and managed hosting turned the weakness into the product.

author: bradyo
cardQuote: Yeah, this title is currently overadvertising the product... this seems to just stitch a "push" system to Postgrest for now (with no auth to boot).
quote:
Yeah, this title is currently overadvertising the product. Without even getting into the non-OLTP DB parts of Firebase, Hasura is much further along towards being a Firebase replacement. It already handles auth and a basic admin UI for both the schema and data. I respect the vision and welcome more competition, but this seems to just stitch a "push" system to Postgrest for now (with no auth to boot).

Hasura also some limited support for generated multi-table transactional APIs, which Postgrest doesn't. Meanwhile, Firebase supports arbitrary read-modify-write transactions.

This team has its work cut out for them and I can see a fierce competition with Hasura and Firebase.
storyTitle: Supabase (YC S20) – An open source Firebase alternative
outcomeDetail: Supabase added auth, storage, edge functions, and a managed Postgres platform. By 2025 it had more than 4 million developers and a $5B valuation.
note: The launch build really was a realtime layer over PostgREST. Supabase closed the auth and platform gaps, then rode the AI-coding boom.

author: PurpleRamen
cardQuote: Looks like a sleek and powerful interface, but at end seems to be just another kitchensink for manual input. No scripting or other automation and service-API is still in work.
quote:
Looks like a sleek and powerful interface, but at end seems to be just another kitchensink for manual input. No scripting or other automation and service-API is still in work.

Im always a bit surprised that programmer invest such an amount of time into recreating the same software again and again. Notes&Task-Manager are all more or less the same, and most of them are not something which a programmer really should use. Those people are handling code and data for other people as natural as a cook his knife. And yet when it comes to their own data they always go for the stale and static, the dumb solution which can is so different from their normal self. Why is that?
storyTitle: Notion – All-in-one workspace for notes, tasks, wikis, and databases
outcomeDetail: Notion became the default all-in-one workspace for notes, docs, wikis, and databases, passed 100 million users, and was valued at $10B in 2021.
note: The missing API and automation were real gaps. Notion shipped its API in 2021 and turned the kitchensink into a platform.

quote:

storyTitle: Show HN: Firebase, a scalable real-time backend
outcome: Acquired by Google in 2014. Core of Google's app platform.
outcomeDetail: Firebase added auth, hosting, and functions, and Google bought it in 2014. It became the default backend for millions of mobile and web apps.
note: The sarcasm targeted an overstuffed pitch. Firebase actually shipped the hard parts: sync, offline caching, and auth. Google paid for it.

author: dreamdu5t
cardQuote: I've been doing "application-scale" development using JavaScript for 5 years... Not once did I think "gee my development process would be better if I had rigid typing." The notion is laughable.
quote:
Poor state of JavaScript development? By what measure?

I've been doing "application-scale" development using JavaScript for 5 years... Not once did I think "gee my development process would be better if I had rigid typing." The notion is laughable.

The lack of rigid typing and classes is by design. This is a feature not a bug. I honestly wonder about a programmer's understanding of JavaScript if they say things like "JS lacks classes!" - I'm not sure they understand JavaScript.
storyTitle: Why does TypeScript have be the answer to anything?
outcome: One of the most-used languages on GitHub.
outcomeDetail: TypeScript became the default for large JavaScript codebases and now ranks among the most-used languages on GitHub. Its optional types made adoption incremental.
note: Plenty of developers still prefer plain JavaScript. TypeScript won the enterprise, the tooling ecosystem, and most new framework templates anyway.

author: smrtinsert
cardQuote: The current fad of quasi declarative web components looks like early Ext to me, and I think everyone knows how that turned out.
quote:
The current fad of quasi declarative web components looks like early Ext to me, and I think everyone knows how that turned out.

I really wish we took it back to a document approach. True REST, everywhere! That's new and novel. Frameworks that build in behaviors with static html - that's just a poor mans gui toolkit. I suppose the web will have go through the task of figuring out its just another in a long line of mistakes. It's like people want to rebuild xslt but badly.
storyTitle: React, a JavaScript library for building user interfaces
outcome: Used by millions of sites; the default UI library for a generation.
outcomeDetail: React's component model became the default way to build web UIs, spawned React Native, and is used by millions of sites. The JSX bet paid off.
note: React was not another Ext: it separated rendering from the DOM and made components composable. The fad became the baseline.

author: kylebrown
cardQuote: The ethereum proposal is the most technical yet. Hopefully it sets a new minimum bar in the market for crowd-funded vaporware (I'm highly skeptical of them all).
quote:
I would rather see an actual, functional product take off (even without miners). The resistance to Ripple just enables an endless series of me-too fundraisers.

The ethereum proposal is the most technical yet. Hopefully it sets a new minimum bar in the market for crowd-funded vaporware (I'm highly skeptical of them all).
outcome: Second-largest cryptocurrency; spot Ether ETFs launched in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Ethereum shipped in 2015, survived hard forks and repeated boom-bust cycles, and became the base layer for DeFi, NFTs, and DAOs. It is the second-largest cryptocurrency.
note: Calling a whitepaper and a pre-mine vaporware was a fair read in 2014. The network shipped, and the developer ecosystem became the moat.

storyTitle: Slack raises $120M Led by Google Ventures and KPCB at $1.12B Valuation
outcomeDetail: Slack turned team chat into a platform, survived competition from Microsoft Teams, and was acquired by Salesforce for $27.7B in 2021.
note: Judging Slack as a static UI missed the real product: search, integrations, and cross-device state. The zoom bug did not define the category.

author: sedachv
cardQuote: So you don't entirely disagree with a bunch of people who have failed to find this imaginary demand, but you think the demand is there?... The demand for an Access-like or "better spreadsheet" product is all of the "Oh yeah, it sounds cool" variety that never results in sales.
quote:
> Access is great as a personal, single-user database, but how much software has been written to expand it past that limitation in small businesses?

There were (and in all probability still are) many multi-user Access projects in use by small businesses.

> I don't entirely disagree with your comment, but I do think there's room and demand in the market for something like AirTable.

So you don't entirely disagree with a bunch of people who have failed to find this imaginary demand, but you think the demand is there? There is demand for business applications for verticals, and for general ERP functions like timesheets and payroll. The demand for an Access-like or "better spreadsheet" product is all of the "Oh yeah, it sounds cool" variety that never results in sales.
storyTitle: Show HN: Airtable, a real-time spreadsheet-database hybrid
outcomeDetail: Airtable turned spreadsheets into lightweight apps and became a unicorn. It is used by hundreds of thousands of organizations, from marketing teams to Fortune 500 ops.
note: It did not replace Excel. It captured the spreadsheet users who needed a database, and that turned out to be a very large market.

author: abalone
cardQuote: This echoes Asana and a lot of the "HTML native" product efforts. Which have mostly failed as a technical approach and resulted in a return to platform native apps.
quote:
The main differentiator and focus of the post is "we're making this run in the browser". But nowhere does it explain why that's better for designers. You don't need it to power collaboration features.

This echoes Asana and a lot of the "HTML native" product efforts. Which have mostly failed as a technical approach and resulted in a return to platform native apps.[1] What's different this time?

Meanwhile this prompts amazed reactions from folks who are technically impressed with how far it pushes the browser. But that was the case with prior HTML native efforts too. It distracts from a critique of the actual product features.

I'd like to see a more head to head comparison with popular tools like Sketch. Maybe the built in team collaboration is better than, say, a companion app like Zeplin. But the implementation details don't really matter to customers.

[1] https://blog.asana.com/2014/07/mobile-plans/
storyTitle: Launch of Figma, a collaborative interface design tool
outcome: Adobe's $20B deal was blocked; used by 95% of the Fortune 500.
outcomeDetail: Figma's browser-native multiplayer canvas became the default interface-design tool. Adobe's $20B acquisition was blocked by regulators in 2023, and Figma kept growing.
note: The browser was the collaboration layer, not a cost-saving compromise. Multiplayer editing made Figma's web-first architecture the advantage.

outcome: Open weights; a global fine-tuning and image-generation ecosystem.

author: oefrha

You can find that kind of user on HN.
storyTitle: ChatGPT: Optimizing language models for dialogue
outcome: 100M users in two months. The fastest-growing consumer app.
outcomeDetail: ChatGPT reached 100 million users in about two months and made chat the default interface for language models. It triggered a trillion-dollar AI infrastructure race.
note: The know-it-all comparison was funny and partly fair. ChatGPT became useful precisely because it was a fluent generalist that could be corrected, not an oracle.

author: catlover76
cardQuote: Cursor would be more promising if it wasn't just a VS Code fork that lags behind upstream VSCode and has broken extensions as a result.
quote: Cursor would be more promising if it wasn't just a VS Code fork that lags behind upstream VSCode and has broken extensions as a result. It has other minor bugs and glitchiness as well, and its main selling point atm, that the LLM gets your entire codebase as context, also isn't reliable with an even moderately-sized codebase.
outcomeDetail: Cursor started as a VS Code fork and became one of the fastest-growing software companies in history, raising at a $29.3B valuation in November 2025 after crossing $1B in annualized revenue.
note: Forking VS Code was the distribution strategy, not the moat. The AI-native editing loop and codebase context became the reason to switch.
